name: Flat iron (hair straightener)
lead: A flat iron, also called a hair straightener, is a heated styling tool with two plates that clamp and glide along sections of hair to straighten or reshape them. It is used to smooth curly or wavy hair, and also to add bends or loose waves [1].

According to Wikipedia, heat straightening works by breaking hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex, which can re-form when the hair is exposed to moisture, and overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage [1]. A laboratory study with an automated iron found that repeated ironing at temperatures from 120 to 175 degrees Celsius produced irreversible straightening in curly hair, with a role for silicone products in the process [3]. Published safety research on flat irons themselves concerns mainly burns; larger epidemiological studies of hair straightening concern chemical relaxers rather than heated irons [4][5][6].

paras: Most flat irons use ceramic plates; lower-priced models have a single ceramic coating and higher-priced ones use several layers or solid ceramic. Later electric and ceramic models added adjustable heat settings and different plate sizes [1]. Some models run on butane or batteries, and some have an automatic shut-off to reduce fire risk [1].

Heated metal tools for straightening date to the 1870s, when French hairdresser Marcel Grateau introduced them, and hot combs were popularized in the early twentieth century by Madam C.J. Walker [1]. A patent issued on 14 December 1909 to Isaac K. Shero for two flat irons heated and pressed together is described as the first hair straightener [1]. Ceramic straightening brushes were patented in 2013 and the DAFNI brand released the first in 2015 [1].

Heat softens hair so that its hydrogen bonds can be reshaped while the hair is held straight. Experimental work with an automated iron controlled temperature, contact force and gliding speed and examined keratin changes after repeated cycles at 120-175 degrees Celsius, finding irreversible straightening of curly hair [3]. Wikipedia notes that moisture can restore the original shape of the hair when the bonds re-form [1].

Flat irons are widely used to straighten and smooth hair, and the laboratory work above shows a measurable straightening effect with heat [3]. In appearance communities the tool is also used for waves or bends; one looksmax.org user shared a photo after using a wide flat iron to give his hair a slight wave, and a respondent said it looked better and suggested a loose perm instead, while the poster said the style made his hairline look less high [7].

No clinical trial of heated flat irons was found. Related human research concerns chemical hair straighteners rather than heated plates: a 30-participant clinical study of chemical straightening and hair structure [6], and Sister Study cohort analyses of straightener and relaxer use in relation to cancers and fibroids [4][5]. Heat straightening has been examined in laboratory work [3] and in a forensic burn study [8].

The plates become hot enough to cause contact burns. A forensic study of two cases of children with second-degree burns from straightener plates used experiments on pig skin to characterize the injuries [8]. Other research has examined how heated straightening affects drug content measured in hair samples [9][10], and a building-air study measured siloxane emissions during hair care product use [11].

Epidemiological studies on hair straightening and cancer or uterine fibroid outcomes generally concern chemical straighteners and relaxers, not heated irons; they are sometimes discussed alongside flat irons. Both analyses used data from the Sister Study cohort [4][5]. A separate 30-patient study found that chemical straightening increased hair smoothness and shine while the hair structure was examined for damage [6].

card.summary: Heated clamp plates that straighten or wave hair; the effect is real but temporary and heat damage and burns are the documented downsides.
card.aka: flat iron, hair straightener, flatiron, hair iron
card.note: Overuse of heat can damage hair; plates can cause contact burns.

quick.overview:
A flat iron uses two heated plates to straighten curly or wavy hair, and can also be used to add waves. It is a standard styling tool and its basic effect is well established.

The straightened shape is not permanent in the same way as chemical treatments: encyclopedic sources say moisture can restore the original shape, although repeated high-heat ironing has been shown in a lab study to straighten curly hair irreversibly.
quick.mechanism: Heat lets hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex be reshaped while the hair is held straight; they can re-form when the hair gets damp.
quick.risks: Overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot plates can cause contact burns, including in children. Large studies linking hair straighteners to cancers or fibroids mostly concern chemical relaxers rather than heat tools.
